Voir ou ne pas voir un dictateur en pein: To See or Not to See a Dictator in Paint
« Je suis assez favorable à l’idée de re: “I’m quite in favour of rethinking what is celebrated in public space”
Lorsqu’ils arrivent à Montréal pour la p: When they arrive in Montréal for the first time, Italians who visit the church in Little Italy freeze in front of the fresco that adorns the vault of Notre-Dame-de-la-Défense. The painting of Benito Mussolini alongside Pope Pius XI, angels and religious figures shocks filmmaker Giovanni Princigalli, who decided to settle in Montréal in 2003.
Qu’ils soient arrivés à Montréal il y a: Whether they arrived in Montréal 10 or 60 years ago, members of the Italian-Montréal community are now mobilizing to have a plaque added to the church explaining the glorification of the dictator in a place of worship in the city.
« On ne veut pas retirer la fresque, on: “We don’t want to remove the fresco, we want to contextualize it to do justice to the Catholic and Italian community, the one that is tolerant and that was a victim of fascism,” says Mr. Princigalli, who is one of the instigators of a petition calling for such a plaque to be added. The view is shared by Université de Montréal Italian history professor Luca Sollai, who arrived in Montréal in 2013.
Fondée en 1910 pour la communauté italie: Founded in 1910 for Montréal’s Italian community, the Notre-Dame-de-la-Défense parish commissioned the Mussolini fresco from painter Guido Nincheri, who carried it out from 1930 to 1933. The work evokes the Lateran Treaty – concluded in 1929 between the Holy See and the Italian government, represented by Mussolini – which led to the creation of the Vatican City State.
À l’époque, plusieurs Italo-Canadiens se: At the time, many Italian Canadians felt like second-class citizens, and their patriotism was heightened by the propaganda operations of Italian consulates in the diaspora, explains Professor Sollai.
Les origines populaires du chef d’État f: The head of state’s humble origins encouraged identification with him and support among the Italian diaspora in North America, which was then rather regional in character. “Mussolini was a cultural model in which the Italian community could see itself. Its goal was not to support fascism; it simply felt protected by this figure,” adds Mr. Sollai.
Aujourd’hui, un fascicule placé à l’entr: Today, a booklet placed at the entrance of the church, written in French, English and Italian, explains that the fresco was completed before Mussolini’s pact with Hitler. “The fresco can be understood through an analysis of the historical context of the 1930s,” it reads. “Apart from occasional visitors, the church’s parishioners no longer look toward Mussolini.
Désormais, il s’agit d’une simple donnée: It is now simply a historical fact,” the document also states. But that does not satisfy Mr. Sollai, who would like a more rigorous contextualization than the one offered by the neighbourhood church.
« Plusieurs hommes d’État dans les année: “Several statesmen in the 1930s viewed fascism favourably, but that doesn’t change the fact that we were talking about a dictatorship as early as the 1920s. It’s clear that the reality of the time matters, but historically, the dictatorship goes back well before the painting of the fresco,” he explains.
Il cite en exemple le prêtre antifascist: He cites the example of the anti-fascist priest Don Giovanni Minzoni, murdered by fascists in 1923. Italo Balbo, one of the fascist leaders shown on the fresco, is suspected of having ordered the killing.
Le professeur d’architecture Fabrizio Ga: Architecture professor Fabrizio Gallanti, who arrived in Montréal in 2011, flatly refuses to set foot in Notre-Dame-de-la-Défense church. “This is not a figure who belongs in public space,” he thunders. “I understand the context, but it’s been 70 years! I find it rather strange that this presence has been maintained for so long,” he adds, pointing out that displaying a fascist symbol in a public space has been prohibited by law in Italy since 1952.
Dans la foulée du déboulonnement de plus: In the wake of the toppling of several statues of colonialist figures around the world since the death of George Floyd, Mr. Gallanti believes the story of the Mussolini fresco is intertwined with the current context, but can also be read on its own. Born in Genoa, the birthplace of Christopher Columbus, Mr. Gallanti says he would like to see his fellow citizens take down the monuments honouring this “sad figure.”
« Je suis assez favorable à l’idée de re: “I’m quite in favour of rethinking what is celebrated in public space,” he tells us. For Carlo Rosati, who landed in Montréal in 1960, the part of the fresco devoted to Mussolini has to go. “Why still have the image of that person? Seeing him in a church, I find it outrageous; if it’s removed, it’s for the best for the image of the Catholic Church.” He believes the fresco drives young people away from religion. “Who was Mussolini? Some say this fresco is part of history, but he was no Michelangelo, he has no place in the church,” he insists.
Du côté de l’église paroissiale, le père: On the parish church’s side, Father Gennuso did not wish to speak to us about the fresco. Instead, it was Pier Luigi Colleoni who responded to our interview request. A high school art history teacher, catechist and member of the board of directors of the Notre-Dame-de-la-Défense parish, he sometimes gives guided tours of the church. One Saturday morning, before a funeral, he offered us his analysis of Guido Nincheri’s fresco. The work has three levels. The bottom part represents the Church Militant, that is, the living; the middle, the saints; and the third, at the top, the divine.
Sur la première section au centre, on vo: In the first section, at the centre, we see Pope Pius XI, the future Pope Pius XII, the archbishop and bishop of Montréal at the time, as well as the parish priest of the day. On the left, priests and nuns stand alongside Black children – representing the missionary work of the Catholic Church in Africa.
À droite, on trouve des « gloires italie: On the right, there are “Italian glories,” including Nobel laureate Guglielmo Marconi and explorer Amedeo di Savoia-Aosta. But above all, we see Benito Mussolini on horseback in the presence of the four important figures of the fascist party, the quadrumvirs: Michele Bianchi, Emilio De Bono, Cesare Maria De Vecchi and Italo Balbo.
En 1940, durant la Deuxième Guerre mondi: In 1940, during the Second World War, when Canada declared war on Italy, Montréal firefighters came to the church to destroy the part of the fresco depicting Mussolini.
La communauté a cependant réussi à négoc: The community, however, managed to negotiate with them and prevented its destruction by covering it with a sheet. That part remained covered until the 1950s, explains Pier Luigi Colleoni. “Some call it Mussolini’s church, others call it the Dante church. The people in the community, who have a sense of belonging to the church, don’t look at Mussolini, he’s not the centre of their attention. The centre of attention is the figure of Christ,” Mr. Colleoni tells us from the doorstep. He believes Mussolini should remain on the fresco for historical and artistic reasons, as well as for the originality the work gives the church.
« Je dis toujours que Mussolini, c’est u: “I always say that Mussolini is an anecdote. Our church is a parish, we come here to pray because we are a Christian community,” he says.
M. Colleoni n’est donc ni en faveur de l: Mr. Colleoni is therefore in favour of neither the petition nor the addition of a plaque. In his view, the booklet at the entrance of the church is enough. “People who usually come to the church know the situation. Visitors, when they arrive and find the booklet, can understand that it’s only a remnant of history.”
Salvatore Martire, installé à Montréal d: Salvatore Martire, who has lived in Montréal since 1960, supports the petition. He tells us that almost 25 years ago, at a funeral, he saw members of the community enter the church making the fascist salute and praising Mussolini. The parish guide, somewhat hesitantly, also confides that he has come face to face with pro-fascists who came to the church to honour the dictator’s memory.
« Je sais qu’il y a des touristes qui vi: “I know there are tourists who come from Italy and have sympathies for fascism. And I know they come here to glorify the memory of Mussolini. The people I’ve welcomed are surprised to learn that we don’t share their enthusiasm for fascism and that we’re not keeping the fresco because we’re fascists or because we worship Mussolini,” says Mr. Colleoni.
Martire aimerait pour sa part qu’on expl: Mr. Martire, for his part, would like the reasons for Mussolini’s presence in the Italian parish’s fresco to be explained. “Whether the fresco stays in the church or not, it’s all the same to me, but I think that if it’s kept, Mussolini’s history has to be explained; people need to know what he did,” he whispers to us over the phone in Italian. “Young people who were born after the war should at least know who this figure above their heads in church is,” says this adviser to the Calabrian community of Canada.
Giuliana (nom fictif), une Italienne de: Giuliana (not her real name), a 30-year-old Italian woman, often went to the church with her grandmother. “This church is kind of the pillar of Montréal’s Italian community. Personally, I never really noticed Mussolini on the fresco and I don’t think people in the community go there because they support him,” she confides, while wishing to remain anonymous. “I lived in Italy and I can understand the shock for some Italians who arrive here.
Mais ce sont des gens éduqués. Il est im: But these are educated people. It’s important to understand the life experiences of the Italian immigrants who came here in the 1930s. They didn’t have much education, they were poor people.
Aujourd’hui, nous avons le privilège de: Today, we have the privilege of taking an interest in this, but our grandparents didn’t have the luxury of asking questions,” she adds. Giuliana admits she is in favour of the petition, but doesn’t know whether she wants to get married in this church. “I don’t think a fascist who supported Hitler should be on the ceiling of our church, but we also have to understand the context of the time,” she concludes.
Le comité de la pétition demande l’ajout: The petition committee is calling for explanatory plaques on the dictator Benito Mussolini written by historians, a rewrite of the church’s booklet on the fresco, a commemorative plaque in memory of Don Giovanni Minzoni, and a commemorative plaque outside for all the Canadian soldiers who died in Italy during the Second World War.
Le comité recueille actuellement des sig: The committee is currently gathering signatures before presenting its petition to Canadian Heritage and the City of Montréal.
Patrimoine Canada n’avait pas répondu à: Canadian Heritage had not responded to our interview requests at the time of writing. The petition is circulating among various personalities, including from the political world, and will be put online shortly.
